subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Viral encephalitis is inflammation of the brain caused by viruses, presenting with fever, headache, altered consciousness, seizures, or focal deficits. Prompt recognition, appropriate testing, and antiviral therapy are essential to reduce mortality and neurological damage.

sections.p: Encephalitis results from viral invasion of brain parenchyma, triggering immune-mediated injury. Clinically it mimics meningitis but with prominent neurologic dysfunction.
b: Fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures
Rapid progression can lead to coma or death

sections.p: Neurotropic viruses cross the blood‑brain barrier via hematogenous spread, neuronal retrograde transport, or direct invasion after trauma.
b: HSV‑1: DNA virus, latency in trigeminal ganglion
Rabies: RNA virus, transports via peripheral nerves

sections.p: Routes include mosquito bites, respiratory droplets, animal bites, and reactivation from latency.
b: Mosquitoes (JE, West Nile) – endemic in tropics

sections.p: Acute viral encephalitis presents with a triad: fever, altered consciousness, and focal neurologic signs. Severity is staged by Glasgow Coma Scale and presence of seizures or brain herniation.
b: Severe: GCS ≤8, brainstem signs, risk of death

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with targeted investigations; early lumbar puncture and neuro‑imaging are critical.

t.b: Pleocytosis (mostly lymphocytes), normal/ mildly elevated protein, normal glucose; if unavailable, rely on serum PCR and imaging
Positive PCR confirms diagnosis; negative PCR does not rule out early infection
Temporal lobe hyperintensity (HSV), thalamic/brainstem lesions (JE); if MRI unavailable, CT may show edema

sections.p: Antiviral therapy targets the most likely pathogen; supportive care prevents secondary injury.
b: IV acyclovir for suspected HSV‑1 (covers most common sporadic cause)
Supportive: airway protection, seizure control, intracranial pressure monitoring
If HSV ruled out, consider ribavirin for rabies exposure (post‑exposure prophylaxis)
Vaccination: JE vaccine in endemic areas, rabies pre‑exposure vaccine for high‑risk workers

sections.p: Key points examiners love: most common sporadic cause, diagnostic CSF findings, first‑line antiviral, and distinguishing features of HSV vs JE vs rabies.
b: HSV‑1: temporal lobe involvement, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, treat with acyclovir
JE: mosquito‑borne, thalamic lesions, prevent with vaccine
Rabies: hydrophobia, Babes‑Mollaret nodules, fatal without prophylaxis

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening consciousness, new seizures, focal neurological deficit, signs of brain herniation

faq.q: What is the most common cause of sporadic viral encephalitis?
Why is a normal CSF glucose not reassuring in viral encephalitis?
faq.a: Viruses typically do not consume glucose, so normal glucose does not exclude infection.
Empirically, as soon as HSV encephalitis is suspected, before PCR results are available.

exam: Explain the pathogenesis of viral encephalitis in three steps.
List the CSF findings typical of viral encephalitis and their diagnostic significance.
Describe the first‑line treatment for HSV encephalitis and why it is preferred over other antivirals.
